title: The suffering ummah
hookLine: wars, refugees and persecution today, and Muslim charities working amid them

lines: THEY CAN FILL THE NEXT BOX.
cards: Rice, lentils, oil, a blanket, soap, a small bag of dates. Volunteers in mismatched gloves are packing them into boxes in a borrowed warehouse.
Someone tapes, someone labels, someone's phone keeps buzzing with news from a place most of them have never seen. The boxes are going to people who left home with what they could carry.
Nobody in the warehouse can stop the war that sent them running. They can fill the next box. Today: the suffering ummah.

teach.b: Ummah is the word for the community of believers, all Muslims everywhere, across every border. And in our time, parts of that body are hurting badly: war, displacement, refugee camps, persecution for faith or ethnicity.

This lesson won't take sides in any conflict or rank anyone's pain. It looks at one teaching, and what people do with it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, gave a picture of how believers belong to one another.
It is reported in Sahih Muslim: the believers, in their love and mercy and kindness to one another, are like one body.

teach.h: ONE BODY: WHEN ONE PART ACHES.
teach.b: When one part of it aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever. Not sympathy from a distance.
Fever. That's why news from one corner of the world can keep someone awake on the other side of it. And the picture asks for more than feeling.

Across the Muslim world and in Muslim communities elsewhere, it has been turned into work: zakat committees, mosque food drives, large charities that run clinics, wells and shelters in war zones and after disasters, often alongside the Red Crescent and many others.
Some of these charities say they help anyone in need, whatever their faith.
The Qur'an puts the instruction plainly: "Help ye one another unto righteousness and pious duty."
The body feels the pain. Then it does the next small thing.

how: Muslims give zakat and voluntary charity, often through mosques and Muslim relief organizations that send food, medicine and shelter to people affected by war and disaster, and appeals are common at Friday prayers and in Ramadan.

o: the worldwide community of all Muslim believers
a single Muslim nation under one government
the local congregation of one mosque

games.q: the suffering ummah — tap the pairs.
p: when one part aches, all answer

s: the hadith says believers should feel sorry from a distance
it says the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever.
the Qur'an tells believers to help one another
Qur'an 5:2: "Help ye one another unto righteousness and pious duty."

games.q: you're in the warehouse. the news on your phone is terrible and you can't change any of it. what do you do?
o: argue about whose fault it is.
games.why: the body picture asks for more than feeling: it turns fever into work, one box at a time.

practice: Bring to mind people who have had to leave home, a family on a road, a child in a camp, someone waiting at a border, and don't picture anyone you can't bear to; keep it gentle. With each out-breath, hold one of them for a moment.
If you pray, ask God's mercy for them in your own words; if not, simply hold them as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Ummah, the worldwide community of believers that the Prophet pictured as one body, feeling fever when any part of it aches. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a community; for Muslims, the community of all believers.

carryVoice: Your line: the body feels the pain. Feeling it is where care begins. Be gentle with yourself today.

sources.q: Help ye one another unto righteousness and pious duty.
